mentl/5ff6b5b:
Priority served: Morgan's question -- why does a frontier sweep not take two
minutes. Answered with numbers, and the answer retracts the plan I gave him
one turn earlier.

MEASURED. 4:57.64 wall for 368 legs over 149 compiler spawns, 99% CPU on ONE
core, 257s of it user time. Real work, uniformly spread -- not a few legs
blocking on something.

THE COST IS NOT INSTANTIATION AND IT IS NOT CONCURRENCY. The same wheel on a
bare stdin fixture with no lib linked: 0.040s. On a manifest-linked fixture:
0.754s. Instantiation plus a genuine compile is 40ms; the other ~715ms is
RE-DERIVING THE PRELUDE, paid 149 times before each five-line fixture is
looked at. PLAN 8 already measured the JIT at ~20ms, which said what the cost
is NOT; this says what it is.

THE PARALLELISM PLAN IS RETRACTED. Running 149 redundant derivations eight at
a time hides the waste behind cores instead of deleting it, which is the fix
direction the Carried-Truth Law forbids. It also carried a hazard worth
recording: pass() and fail() increment shell counters in the CURRENT shell
across 2707 inline lines, so backgrounding a leg loses its increment and the
gate reports fewer legs while still printing 0 red. An arbiter that silently
under-reports is worse than a slow one.

THE NAMED FIX ALREADY EXISTS. Hb.persist.module-image-cache (band O) -- the
derived graph image persisted and reloaded, keyed by source hash plus
transitive dep hashes, which is 4-4's persist-as-memcpy applied to exactly
this. One derivation, 149 loads. The resident session is the same fact at
session scope, and this gate has legs TESTING that capability while not using
it.

And what not to do: narrow the sweep. That was proposed and refused the same
day; the coverage is not the problem, the re-derivation is.

Landed docs-only, so the hook is the arbiter and I did not re-run the board
by hand -- the first iteration under the corrected step 6.

mentl/5fb0694:
When an if/else condition is a compile-time constant, the compiler
emits only the taken branch:
  if true { 42 } else { 99 }  →  just LoadInt 42
  if 1 > 2 { a } else { b }  →  just b (1>2 folded to false first)

Combined with constant folding, this creates a cascade: constant
expressions fold → comparison becomes constant → dead branch eliminated.
Three optimizations, one knowledge advantage: the compiler knows more.

two-top/5f163e1:
The web entry (COMPLETION_PLAN P.5, NORTH N3): web/index.html reads
#watch=<id>, fetches the tape from the drop, and hands the bytes to a
wasm-bindgen web_start; once the app reaches the Title, the tape rolls
through the theater's own projector — the browser shows the real
presentation because it runs the real game. A bare visit boots to the
Title. web.yml builds the bundle on push (bindgen CLI version read out
of Cargo.lock so it can never skew from the crate) and deploys it to
GitHub Pages with the assets dir beside it.

Three walls fell between compiling and rendering, each named by
narrowing the console. ggrs times frames with instant, which without
its js feature is an extern env.now — the lone unresolved import; its
own wasm-bindgen feature fixes it. A panic then surfaced as a bare
unreachable with no message: the first-draft wasm logging installed a
discarding fmt layer whose default timer stamps SystemTime::now(),
which panics on wasm32-unknown — so the panic hook re-panicked inside
itself; wasm now installs no subscriber and console_error_panic_hook
speaks instead. The named panic was wgpu's: the curated bevy feature
list carried no browser graphics backend; webgl2 joins via a
wasm-scoped dep for reach (every mobile browser), WebGPU later.

Verified headless on this box: tape_drop up, canonical tape posted,
chrome loads #watch=<id>, and the screenshot shows the Anchor mid
countdown with both duelists at their spawns and the theater controls
live. Known caveat: audio stays suspended until a user gesture (the
browser autoplay policy); the visuals do not wait.
stoop/5f88656:
Three forms for "a thing I wrote down": a log line with a tag, a journal
entry with a title and an author picker, a project with a title and a
description. They are one stream now. A scrap is a line, or a page with
a title, or a photograph, by somebody, on a day. The tag picker is gone;
nobody was choosing between moment, quote, idea and link. Enter keeps a
scrap, Shift-Enter makes a line.

Older notebooks fold in on the way through migrate: journal entries and
projects arrive as scraps with their titles and keep their ids, so a
backup written last month merges without doubling anything, and the two
collections are then always empty. The backup no longer writes them.
Every old hash (log, journal, projects, notebook) opens the scraps.

The desk pulls from one source. A scrap with a title, or a long one, is
a piece of its own; the short ones run together as one piece the way a
log column always did, and the first photograph among them rides with
it. The couples' skeleton the app was born with is gone from the surface
and from the model, and the fragment is seven kilobytes lighter.
